summary: The note describes the European Central Bank, the central bank for the euro, which sets monetary policy for the eurozone and is headquartered in Frankfurt. It covers the bank's mandate (price stability), its main tasks, its role in the 2007 subprime crisis, the structure of its Executive Board, and debate over responses to the European debt crisis that began in late 2009.
one_line: The European Central Bank, based in Frankfurt, runs monetary policy for the euro and has price stability as its primary mandate.
key_facts: The European Central Bank (ECB) is the central bank for the euro and administers monetary policy of the eurozone, which consists of 19 EU member states.
The capital stock of the European Central Bank is owned by the central banks of all 28 EU member states.
The Treaty of Amsterdam established the European Central Bank in 1998, and it is headquartered in Frankfurt, Germany.
As of 2015 the President of the ECB is Mario Draghi, former governor of the Bank of Italy and former managing director of the Goldman Sachs international division (2002 -- 2005).
Under Article 2 of the Statute of the ECB, the primary objective of the European Central Bank is to maintain price stability within the Eurozone.
Under Article 16 of its Statute, the ECB has the exclusive right to authorise the issuance of euro banknotes.
Member states can issue euro coins, but the amount must be authorised by the ECB beforehand.
During the subprime mortgage crisis, the European Central Bank loaned billions of euros to banks to stabilise the financial system.
In December 2007, the ECB decided in conjunction with the Federal Reserve System under a programme called Term auction facility to improve dollar liquidity in the eurozone.
The Executive Board is responsible for implementing monetary policy, as defined by the Governing Council, and for the day-to-day running of the bank.

The Executive Board is composed of the President (currently Mario Draghi), the Vice-President (currently Vitor Constâncio) and four other members, all appointed for non-renewable terms of eight years.
The Executive Board normally meets every Tuesday.
The European Central Bank had stepped up the buying of member nations' debt in response to the crisis of 2010.
The German government resisted proposals for a collective European bond issue that would let the central bank buy a European version of US Treasury bills.
The European debt crisis began from late 2009 after Greece's new elected government stopped masking its true indebtedness and budget deficit.
